tagline: Prairie miles connect mission churches and towns shaped by the Dawson Railway
intro: La Frontera del Llano follows NM 39 across northeastern New Mexico as a New Mexico State Scenic Byway. The New Mexico Tourism Department presents the Abbott-to-Logan drive through its grasslands, mission churches and state parks. Shortgrass prairie is the dominant vegetation in the Kiowa and adjoining Rita Blanca grasslands, while the Canadian River cuts through the western unit. The grassland mixes public and private land, and nearly all Kiowa National Grassland acreage is leased for cattle grazing.

The corridor’s towns took shape with another transport route: the Dawson Railway, built through Roy in 1902 to carry the line from Tucumcari toward Dawson’s coal fields. Roy moved to meet it, and Mosquero began as a railway water stop. After the rails were removed, Roy’s economy declined. Solano, once Harding County’s largest town, also lost importance when Dawson’s coal mines closed in the 1950s.

Travel southeast from Abbott through the grasslands toward Roy. At Mills, a separate excursion leads west to the Canadian River’s canyon rim. Continue through Roy, Solano and Mosquero; mission churches mark the stretch from Solano to Gallegos. The drive ends at Logan beside the Canadian River country of Ute Lake State Park.

moments.title: Mills Canyon
moments.text: Mills itself lies eleven miles north of Roy on NM 39. Six miles west of Mills, the Canadian River Canyon opens 700 feet deep and more than a mile across. Its red rock and vegetation belong to the western unit of New Mexico’s Kiowa National Grassland. On the canyon floor, ruins mark Melvin Mills’s early-1900s homestead, where he had a home and apple orchard. The community above takes its name from Mills, a rancher and attorney. A primitive campground occupies the rim; the road below accommodates walkers, horses and high-clearance vehicles.

moments.title: Roy
moments.text: Roy’s more than forty city blocks record the extent of its earlier growth. Ranchers Frank and William Roy founded the village; Frank became its first postmaster in 1901 and gave the settlement its name. When the Dawson Railway arrived in 1902, the village relocated to the line serving the coal fields. The move took Roy two miles east of its original location. Incorporation followed in 1916. Removal of the railroad after 1950 brought a significant loss of economic activity. The village now sits off NM 39 in New Mexico’s northeastern plains.

moments.title: Mosquero
moments.text: Mosquero combined a railway water stop with an industry drawn from underground gas. Its dry ice plant used carbon dioxide from wells drilled into the Bravo Dome gas field beneath Harding and Union counties. Benjamin Brown founded the village in 1908, and it developed as a farming, stock-raising and shipping center. The railway, absorbed by Southern Pacific, was removed in 1950; the population dwindled after the dry ice plant was destroyed. NM 39 continues southeast from Mosquero to Logan. The village is Harding County’s seat, with a small portion extending into San Miguel County.

practical: Mills Canyon: The road into the canyon calls for a high-clearance vehicle. (checked 2026-10-11)
